How to Use This Book

This book covers Section B of MTE 4011, which is Tanvir Sir's part of the course. It follows his lecture files: lecture 1 (introduction), MT_Ml_L1 (learning from unlabeled data, K-means), the class notes (CS229 notes: K-means convergence, convexity), MT HAC V3 (hierarchical clustering), MT_kNN_N (KNN), MT_Ml_L (dimensionality reduction) and pcaLectureShort (covariance and PCA). Every chapter has three layers:

  1. Theory: each slide idea rewritten as a complete, exam-ready explanation, with the proofs the slides only mention (K-means convergence, PCA as an eigenvalue problem, the empty-space calculation) written out line by line.
  2. Worked lecture examples: the tomato KNN example, the six-point HAC example (both single and complete linkage) and the PCA toy example are fully recomputed.
  3. Solved past questions: every Section B question from the 2022, 2023 and 2024 term finals, quoted word for word and then answered. Numericals start with a Given Data block and show every arithmetic step.

1. Learning from Unlabeled Data ★★★

1.1 Machine Learning and Its Four Types of Learning

Machine learning is the science, grown out of artificial intelligence, of making computers learn from data rather than from hand-written rules. Arthur Samuel coined the term in 1959. The formal definition used in the lecture is Tom Mitchell's: a computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some task T and performance measure P if its performance at T, as measured by P, improves with experience E. Real-world data (images of cats, fruits under changing light, occlusion and camera angle) varies too much for rule-based programs. This forces a shift to data-driven computing, where data is at the core of every ML project.

TypeData usedGoalExamples
SupervisedInputs and desired outputs, ⟨X,y⟩\langle X,y\rangle⟨X,y⟩Learn a mapping X→yX\to yX→y to predict labels of new inputs (classification) or values (regression)Spam filtering, tumour benign/malignant, house price
UnsupervisedInputs only, X1,…,XpX_1,\dots,X_pX1​,…,Xp​ on nnn observationsDiscover structure: groups (clustering), low-dimensional views (PCA), associationsCustomer segmentation, cocktail-party problem, gene grouping
Semi-supervisedA few labeled + many unlabeled examplesUse the unlabeled data to improve a model trained on the scarce labelsWeb-page or medical-image classification with few annotations
ReinforcementRewards from interaction with an environmentLearn actions that maximise long-term rewardGame playing, robot control

1.2 Labeled and Unlabeled Data

Definitions
Labeled data is data in which every observation is accompanied by the correct output value, the target: a class label or a numerical value. Example: images of animals, each tagged dog, cat or bird.
Unlabeled data is data with input features only and no associated output value. Example: a collection of documents with no predefined categories.

In the supervised setting we have ppp features X1,X2,…,XpX_1,X_2,\dots,X_pX1​,X2​,…,Xp​ measured on nnn observations and a response YYY on the same observations, and the goal is to predict YYY. In the unsupervised setting we have only X1,…,XpX_1,\dots,X_pX1​,…,Xp​. We are not interested in prediction, because there is no response; the goal is to discover interesting things about the measurements. Is there an informative way to visualise the data? Can we discover subgroups among the observations or the variables?

AspectLabeled dataUnlabeled data
ContentFeatures + correct target (xi,yi)(x_i,y_i)(xi​,yi​)Features only xix_ixi​
Cost to obtainHigh: needs human annotation, often by expertsLow: collected automatically (sensors, logs, web)
Quantity availableUsually smallUsually huge
Used bySupervised learning (classification, regression)Unsupervised learning (clustering, dimensionality reduction)
EvaluationEasy: compare predictions with true labels (accuracy, MSE)Hard: no ground truth to compare against
ExampleX-ray images each marked "fracture / normal" by a radiologistMillions of untagged X-ray images in a hospital archive

1.3 What Clustering Is

Definition
Clustering is a broad set of unsupervised techniques for finding subgroups (clusters) in a data set. We partition the observations into distinct groups so that observations within a group are very similar to each other, while observations in different groups are quite different. What "similar" means must be defined, usually through a distance measure, and this is often a domain-specific decision.

Clustering looks for homogeneous subgroups among the observations. The two best-known methods are K-means clustering (Chapter 3), where the number of clusters KKK is fixed in advance, and hierarchical clustering (Chapter 4), which builds a tree of nested clusters (a dendrogram) without fixing KKK. Applications include market segmentation, grouping similar documents or genes, image segmentation, anomaly detection, and grouping sensor signatures of machine faults in mechatronics.

1.4 Solved Questions

2024 · Q5(a)Q1.1 — Define labeled and unlabeled data. Explain why labeled data is expensive. In what scenarios is the labeled data beneficial for machine learning tasks?10Topic: labeled vs unlabeled data

Definitions. Labeled data is data in which each observation carries its correct output (target) value, a class label or a number, e.g. an image of an animal with the tag "cat". Unlabeled data has input features only, with no target, e.g. a folder of untagged animal photos.

Why labeled data is expensive.

  1. Human effort: each example must be annotated manually, one by one. Large data sets need thousands of hours of work.
  2. Expertise: many labels need specialists (radiologists for medical images, engineers for fault signatures, linguists for speech), whose time is costly.
  3. Time: annotation of video, 3-D point clouds or segmentation masks (pixel-level labels) can take minutes to hours per item.
  4. Quality control: labels are noisy and subjective, so several annotators and agreement checks are needed, which multiplies the cost.
  5. Destructive or rare events: some labels need an experiment (a fatigue test to failure) or a rare event (a machine breakdown), which is expensive or slow to observe.
  6. Privacy and legal constraints: medical and personal data need consent and secure handling before anyone can label them.

Scenarios where labeled data is beneficial.

  • Supervised prediction tasks, classification and regression, where the goal is to predict a known quantity for new data: spam detection, disease diagnosis, price or load forecasting, defect detection on a production line.
  • Model evaluation and validation: even unsupervised systems need a labeled test set to measure accuracy objectively.
  • Safety-critical systems (autonomous driving, medical devices) where predictions must be verified against ground truth.
  • Guiding training toward a specific desired output, which unlabeled data alone cannot do.
  • Semi-supervised and transfer learning, where a small labeled set steers a model trained on large unlabeled data.
Source lectureTanvir Sir · L1 – Clustering & unsupervised learning (MT_Ml_L1.pdf, pp. 5–6)
2022 · Q5(a)Q1.2 — What is the difference between labeled data and unlabeled data? What do you mean by clustering?07Topic: labeled vs unlabeled · clustering

Difference: use the comparison table of §1.2 (content, cost, quantity, learning type, evaluation, example). In one line: labeled data consists of pairs (xi,yi)(x_i,y_i)(xi​,yi​) with known targets and drives supervised learning; unlabeled data consists of xix_ixi​ only and is used by unsupervised learning to discover structure.

Clustering is the unsupervised task of partitioning a set of unlabeled observations into groups (clusters) such that observations in the same cluster are similar to one another and dissimilar to those in other clusters. Similarity is measured by a distance such as the Euclidean distance. Examples: K-means and hierarchical agglomerative clustering, used for customer segmentation or grouping similar sensor signals.

2. Convexity in Machine-Learning Optimization ★★★

Almost every learning algorithm is an optimization: training means finding parameters www that minimise a loss f(w)f(w)f(w). Whether that loss is convex decides how easy and how reliable training is.

2.1 Convex Sets and Convex Functions

Definitions
A set SSS is convex if the line segment between any two of its points stays in SSS: x,y∈S ⇒ θx+(1−θ)y∈Sfor all 0≤θ≤1.x,y\in S\ \Rightarrow\ \theta x+(1-\theta)y\in S\qquad\text{for all }0\le\theta\le1.x,y∈S ⇒ θx+(1−θ)y∈Sfor all 0≤θ≤1. A function fff defined on a convex set is convex if, for all x,yx,yx,y and 0≤θ≤10\le\theta\le10≤θ≤1, f(θx+(1−θ)y)≤θf(x)+(1−θ)f(y).f\bigl(\theta x+(1-\theta)y\bigr)\le\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y).f(θx+(1−θ)y)≤θf(x)+(1−θ)f(y). Geometrically: the chord joining any two points on the graph lies on or above the graph. fff is strictly convex if "<" holds whenever x≠yx\ne yx=y and 0<θ<10<\theta<10<θ<1, and concave if −f-f−f is convex.

2.1.1 Tests for convexity

  • First-order: fff is convex iff it lies above all its tangents: f(y)≥f(x)+∇f(x)T(y−x)f(y)\ge f(x)+\nabla f(x)^T(y-x)f(y)≥f(x)+∇f(x)T(y−x) for all x,yx,yx,y.
  • Second-order: one variable, f′′(x)≥0f''(x)\ge0f′′(x)≥0 everywhere. Several variables, the Hessian H(x)\mathbf H(x)H(x) is positive semidefinite for every xxx (all eigenvalues ≥ 0). This is the CS229 statement: "when fff has a Hessian, it is convex iff the Hessian is positive semidefinite".
  • Examples: wTww^TwwTw, exe^xex, ∣x∣|x|∣x∣, −log⁡x-\log x−logx and every linear (affine) function are convex. x3x^3x3, sin⁡x\sin xsinx and x4−2x2x^4-2x^2x4−2x2 are not.
  • Rules: non-negative sums of convex functions are convex; a convex function of an affine map f(Aw+b)f(Aw+b)f(Aw+b) is convex; the maximum of convex functions is convex.

2.2 Why Convexity Is Desirable

Key theorem: for a convex function, every local minimum is a global minimum
Proof. Let x∗x^*x∗ be a local minimum and suppose some yyy has f(y)<f(x∗)f(y)<f(x^*)f(y)<f(x∗). For 0<θ≤10<\theta\le10<θ≤1, the point z=θy+(1−θ)x∗z=\theta y+(1-\theta)x^*z=θy+(1−θ)x∗ satisfies, by convexity, f(z)≤θf(y)+(1−θ)f(x∗)<θf(x∗)+(1−θ)f(x∗)=f(x∗).f(z)\le\theta f(y)+(1-\theta)f(x^*)<\theta f(x^*)+(1-\theta)f(x^*)=f(x^*).f(z)≤θf(y)+(1−θ)f(x∗)<θf(x∗)+(1−θ)f(x∗)=f(x∗). As θ→0\theta\to0θ→0, zzz comes arbitrarily close to x∗x^*x∗ yet has a smaller value, which contradicts local minimality. Hence no such yyy exists. ■\blacksquare■

Consequences for machine learning:

  1. No bad local minima: any minimum an algorithm finds is the best possible solution.
  2. Guaranteed convergence: gradient descent with a suitable learning rate provably converges to the global optimum, with known convergence rates.
  3. Initialisation does not matter: every starting point leads to the same optimum value, so results are reproducible.
  4. Simple optimality test: ∇f(w∗)=0\nabla f(w^*)=0∇f(w∗)=0 is both necessary and sufficient. For constrained problems the KKT conditions are sufficient, and duality can be exploited (as in the SVM dual).
  5. Efficient, reliable solvers: mature algorithms (Newton, interior-point, coordinate descent) solve convex problems quickly, even with millions of variables.
  6. Strict convexity gives a unique solution, which makes the model well defined and easier to interpret.

2.4 Solved Questions

2024 · Q5(b)Q2.1 — Define a convex function and explain why convexity is desirable in optimization.10Topic: convex function

Definition. A function f:Rn→Rf:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb Rf:Rn→R on a convex domain is convex if for every two points x,yx,yx,y and every θ∈[0,1]\theta\in[0,1]θ∈[0,1]:

f(θx+(1−θ)y)≤θf(x)+(1−θ)f(y).f\bigl(\theta x+(1-\theta)y\bigr)\le\theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y).f(θx+(1−θ)y)≤θf(x)+(1−θ)f(y).

The chord between any two points of its graph never lies below the graph (Fig. 2.1, left). Equivalent tests: f′′(x)≥0f''(x)\ge0f′′(x)≥0 for a single variable, or a positive semidefinite Hessian everywhere for several variables. Example: f(w)=w2f(w)=w^2f(w)=w2, since f′′=2>0f''=2>0f′′=2>0. The mean-squared-error loss of linear regression is also convex.

Why it is desirable. Give the proof of §2.2 (local minimum = global minimum) and then the consequences: (1) no spurious local minima, so any minimum found is the best; (2) gradient descent is guaranteed to converge to the global optimum for a suitable step size; (3) the result does not depend on initialisation; (4) ∇f=0\nabla f=0∇f=0 (or KKT) is a sufficient optimality test; (5) fast, reliable solvers exist; (6) strict convexity gives a unique solution. Non-convex problems lack all of these guarantees.

Model flexibilityLimited (linear or kernel models)Very expressive (deep networks)
ExamplesLinear and ridge/lasso regression, logistic regression, SVMNeural networks, K-means, Gaussian-mixture EM, matrix factorisation, t-SNE

Example of each. Convex: linear regression minimises J(w)=12m∥Xw−y∥2J(w)=\tfrac1{2m}\lVert Xw-y\rVert^2J(w)=2m1​∥Xw−y∥2. Its Hessian 1mXTX\tfrac1mX^TXm1​XTX is positive semidefinite, so the normal-equation solution is the global optimum. Non-convex: a two-layer network y^=w2 σ(w1x)\hat y=w_2\,\sigma(w_1x)y^​=w2​σ(w1​x). Swapping two hidden neurons gives a different weight vector with the same loss, so there are several separate minima. Because the minima are separate, the loss cannot be a single bowl, and so it is not convex.

Source lectureTanvir Sir · Class notes (Class_notes (2).pdf, p. 12); Class notes (Class_notes (2).pdf, p. 138) — No direct comparison; convex/non-convex examples scattered in class notes
2023 · Q5(b)Q2.3 — Discuss the impact of non-convexity on gradient based optimization algorithms commonly used in machine learning, such as gradient descent.10Topic: non-convexity and gradient descent

Gradient descent updates wt+1=wt−η∇f(wt)w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta\nabla f(w_t)wt+1​=wt​−η∇f(wt​), following the local slope only. It knows nothing about the global shape of fff. On a non-convex loss this causes:

  1. Getting trapped in local minima: where ∇f=0\nabla f=0∇f=0 in a shallow valley, the updates stop, although a much lower valley exists elsewhere.
  2. Saddle points: points with ∇f=0\nabla f=0∇f=0 that are a minimum along some directions and a maximum along others. In high-dimensional networks these are far more common than local minima. Near them the gradient is tiny, so training slows or stalls.
  3. Plateaus and vanishing gradients: flat regions (e.g. saturated sigmoids) give nearly zero gradient, so progress is extremely slow.
  4. Sensitivity to initialisation: different starting weights converge to different solutions of different quality, so the results are not reproducible.
  5. Learning-rate sensitivity: sharp ravines make a large η\etaη oscillate or diverge and a small η\etaη crawl. No single step size is safe everywhere.
  6. No convergence certificate: reaching ∇f≈0\nabla f\approx0∇f≈0 does not prove optimality, and there is no bound on how far the result is from the global optimum.

Remedies used in practice: stochastic/mini-batch gradients (their noise helps escape saddles and shallow minima); momentum, RMSProp and Adam; learning-rate schedules and warm restarts; careful initialisation (Xavier/He); batch normalisation and ReLU activations (fewer plateaus); several random restarts, keeping the best; and over-parameterisation, which makes most minima nearly equally good.

Source lectureTanvir Sir · Class notes (Class_notes (2).pdf, p. 12); Class notes (Class_notes (2).pdf, p. 138) — Passing remarks only; saddle points and plateaus not covered

3. K-Means Clustering ★★★

K-means is a simple and elegant approach for partitioning a data set into K distinct, non-overlapping clusters. The desired number of clusters KKK must be specified first. The algorithm then assigns each observation to exactly one of the KKK clusters.

3.1 The Objective

Let C1,…,CKC_1,\dots,C_KC1​,…,CK​ be sets of observation indices such that every observation belongs to exactly one cluster: C1∪⋯∪CK={1,…,n}C_1\cup\cdots\cup C_K=\{1,\dots,n\}C1​∪⋯∪CK​={1,…,n} and Ck∩Ck′=∅C_k\cap C_{k'}=\varnothingCk​∩Ck′​=∅. A good clustering has a small within-cluster variation W(Ck)W(C_k)W(Ck​). K-means solves

min⁡C1,…,CK ∑k=1KW(Ck),W(Ck)=1∣Ck∣∑i,i′∈Ck ∑j=1p(xij−xi′j)2.\min_{C_1,\dots,C_K}\ \sum_{k=1}^{K}W(C_k),\qquad W(C_k)=\frac{1}{|C_k|}\sum_{i,i'\in C_k}\ \sum_{j=1}^{p}(x_{ij}-x_{i'j})^2 .C1​,…,CK​min​ k=1∑K​W(Ck​),W(Ck​)=∣Ck​∣1​i,i′∈Ck​∑​ j=1∑p​(xij​−xi′j​)2.

Identity (why the centroid appears). Let xˉk\bar x_kxˉk​ be the mean of cluster CkC_kCk​. Write xi−xi′=(xi−xˉk)−(xi′−xˉk)x_i-x_{i'}=(x_i-\bar x_k)-(x_{i'}-\bar x_k)xi​−xi′​=(xi​−xˉk​)−(xi′​−xˉk​) and expand the square:

∑i,i′∈Ck∥xi−xi′∥2=∑i,i′[∥xi−xˉk∥2+∥xi′−xˉk∥2]−2(∑i(xi−xˉk))T(∑i′(xi′−xˉk)).\sum_{i,i'\in C_k}\lVert x_i-x_{i'}\rVert^2=\sum_{i,i'}\Bigl[\lVert x_i-\bar x_k\rVert^2+\lVert x_{i'}-\bar x_k\rVert^2\Bigr]-2\Bigl(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x_k)\Bigr)^T\Bigl(\sum_{i'}(x_{i'}-\bar x_k)\Bigr).i,i′∈Ck​∑​∥xi​−xi′​∥2=i,i′∑​[∥xi​−xˉk​∥2+∥xi′​−xˉk​∥2]−2(i∑​(xi​−xˉk​))T(i′∑​(xi′​−xˉk​)).

The last bracket is zero because deviations from the mean sum to zero. Each of the first two sums equals ∣Ck∣∑i∥xi−xˉk∥2|C_k|\sum_{i}\lVert x_i-\bar x_k\rVert^2∣Ck​∣∑i​∥xi​−xˉk​∥2. Dividing by ∣Ck∣|C_k|∣Ck​∣:

W(Ck)=2∑i∈Ck∥xi−xˉk∥2.W(C_k)=2\sum_{i\in C_k}\lVert x_i-\bar x_k\rVert^2 .W(Ck​)=2i∈Ck​∑​∥xi​−xˉk​∥2.

So minimising the within-cluster variation is the same as minimising the squared distances to the cluster centroids. This is the distortion function of the class notes:

J(c,μ)=∑i=1n∥x(i)−μc(i)∥2.J(c,\mu)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl\lVert x^{(i)}-\mu_{c^{(i)}}\bigr\rVert^2 .J(c,μ)=i=1∑n​​x(i)−μc(i)​​2.
[KEY IDENTITY]∑i∈C(xi−xˉ)=0\sum_{i\in C}(x_i-\bar x)=0∑i∈C​(xi​−xˉ)=0: deviations from a mean always sum to zero.

3.2 The Algorithm

K-means (Lloyd's algorithm)
  1. Initialise: choose KKK initial centroids μ1,…,μK\mu_1,\dots,\mu_Kμ1​,…,μK​ (e.g. KKK randomly chosen observations), or randomly assign each observation a cluster number 1 to KKK.
  2. Repeat until the assignments stop changing:
    1. Assignment step: for each iii, c(i):=arg⁡min⁡k∥x(i)−μk∥2c^{(i)}:=\arg\min_k\lVert x^{(i)}-\mu_k\rVert^2c(i):=argmink​∥x(i)−μk​∥2 (nearest centroid, Euclidean distance).
    2. Update step: for each kkk, μk:=1∣Ck∣∑i∈Ckx(i)\mu_k:=\dfrac{1}{|C_k|}\sum_{i\in C_k}x^{(i)}μk​:=∣Ck​∣1​∑i∈Ck​​x(i) (mean of the points assigned to kkk).

3.3 Convergence of K-Means

Theorem (class notes, §10)
K-means is guaranteed to converge, in the sense that the distortion JJJ decreases monotonically and the algorithm stops after a finite number of iterations. It converges to a local minimum of JJJ, which need not be the global minimum.

Proof: K-means is coordinate descent on J(c,μ)J(c,\mu)J(c,μ).

  1. The assignment step minimises JJJ over ccc with μ\muμ fixed. J=∑i∥x(i)−μc(i)∥2J=\sum_i\lVert x^{(i)}-\mu_{c^{(i)}}\rVert^2J=∑i​∥x(i)−μc(i)​∥2 is a sum of separate terms, one per observation. Each term is smallest when c(i)c^{(i)}c(i) picks the nearest centroid, which is exactly what the step does. Hence J(cnew,μ)≤J(cold,μ)J(c^{new},\mu)\le J(c^{old},\mu)J(cnew,μ)≤J(cold,μ).
  2. The update step minimises JJJ over μ\muμ with ccc fixed. For cluster kkk only the terms with c(i)=kc^{(i)}=kc(i)=k depend on μk\mu_kμk​. Setting the gradient to zero: ∂∂μk∑i∈Ck∥x(i)−μk∥2=−2∑i∈Ck(x(i)−μk)=0 ⇒ ∣Ck∣ μk=∑i∈Ckx(i) ⇒ μk=1∣Ck∣∑i∈Ckx(i).\frac{\partial}{\partial\mu_k}\sum_{i\in C_k}\lVert x^{(i)}-\mu_k\rVert^2=-2\sum_{i\in C_k}\bigl(x^{(i)}-\mu_k\bigr)=0\ \Rightarrow\ |C_k|\,\mu_k=\sum_{i\in C_k}x^{(i)}\ \Rightarrow\ \mu_k=\frac{1}{|C_k|}\sum_{i\in C_k}x^{(i)}.∂μk​∂​i∈Ck​∑​∥x(i)−μk​∥2=−2i∈Ck​∑​(x(i)−μk​)=0 ⇒ ∣Ck​∣μk​=i∈Ck​∑​x(i) ⇒ μk​=∣Ck​∣1​i∈Ck​∑​x(i). The Hessian is 2∣Ck∣I≻02|C_k|\mathbf I\succ02∣Ck​∣I≻0, so this is the minimum, the mean. Hence J(c,μnew)≤J(c,μold)J(c,\mu^{new})\le J(c,\mu^{old})J(c,μnew)≤J(c,μold).
  3. Monotone and bounded. Every step does not increase JJJ, and J≥0J\ge0J≥0 (a sum of squares). A non-increasing sequence bounded below converges.
  4. Finite termination. There are at most KnK^nKn ways to assign nnn points to KKK clusters, and each assignment determines the centroids and JJJ. JJJ strictly decreases whenever an assignment changes (using a fixed tie-breaking rule), so no clustering can repeat. The algorithm must therefore stop after finitely many iterations, when the assignments no longer change. (In theory, without a tie-breaking rule, JJJ could stay constant while it oscillates between equal-cost clusterings. This is extremely rare.)
  5. Only a local minimum. JJJ is non-convex (the assignments are discrete), so coordinate descent can stop at a clustering that cannot be improved by moving one centroid or one point, yet is not the best overall. ■\blacksquare■
Remedies for bad local minima
  1. Multiple random restarts: run K-means many times from different random initial centroids and keep the clustering with the lowest distortion JJJ (class-notes remedy).
  2. K-means++ initialisation: choose the first centroid at random and each next one with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest chosen centroid. This spreads the starting centroids out.
  3. Better choice of K (elbow or silhouette method), since a wrong KKK produces poor local solutions.
  4. Pre-processing: standardise features and remove or down-weight outliers, which otherwise capture a centroid (see Q3.4).
  5. Split-and-merge / bisecting K-means, or initialising from a hierarchical-clustering result.

3.4 Problems of K-Means and Choosing K

ProblemExplanation
K must be chosen in advanceThe true number of clusters is usually unknown. Use the elbow method (plot JJJ against KKK and pick the bend), the silhouette score, the gap statistic, or domain knowledge.
Sensitive to initialisationDifferent starts converge to different local minima (§3.3).
Sensitive to outliersThe mean is pulled strongly by extreme points. An outlier can take a whole centroid for itself (Q3.4).
Assumes spherical, similar-size clustersEuclidean distance to a centroid fails for elongated, curved (non-convex) or different-density clusters.
Scale dependentA feature measured in large units dominates the distance; features should be standardised.
Numerical data onlyA mean is undefined for categorical data (use K-modes / K-medoids instead).
Hard assignment, possible empty clustersEach point belongs to exactly one cluster, and a centroid may lose all its points.

3.5 Solved Questions

2023 · Q5(c)Q3.1 — Is the K-means clustering algorithm guaranteed to converge? Support your answer with proper mathematical explanation. What will be the remedy if K-means clustering algorithm get stuck in bad local minima?15Topic: convergence proof · remedies

Answer: yes, it is guaranteed to converge, but only to a local minimum. Write the distortion J(c,μ)=∑i∥x(i)−μc(i)∥2J(c,\mu)=\sum_i\lVert x^{(i)}-\mu_{c^{(i)}}\rVert^2J(c,μ)=∑i​∥x(i)−μc(i)​∥2 and give the five-step proof of §3.3: (1) the assignment step minimises JJJ over ccc; (2) the update step minimises JJJ over μ\muμ, with the derivative −2∑(x(i)−μk)=0-2\sum(x^{(i)}-\mu_k)=0−2∑(x(i)−μk​)=0 giving the mean; (3) JJJ is non-increasing and bounded below by 0; (4) finitely many (≤Kn\le K^n≤Kn) partitions, so the algorithm terminates; (5) JJJ is non-convex, so the limit is a local minimum. Then list the remedies from the box in §3.3: multiple random restarts keeping the lowest JJJ, K-means++, a correct choice of K, standardisation and outlier removal, and bisecting or hierarchical initialisation.

Source lectureTanvir Sir · Class notes (Class_notes (2).pdf, pp. 137–138)
2022 · Q5(b)Q3.2 — Is the convergence of K-Means algorithm guaranteed? Support your answer with proper explanation.08Topic: convergence

Yes. K-means performs coordinate descent on the distortion J(c,μ)=∑i∥x(i)−μc(i)∥2J(c,\mu)=\sum_i\lVert x^{(i)}-\mu_{c^{(i)}}\rVert^2J(c,μ)=∑i​∥x(i)−μc(i)​∥2. The assignment step can only lower JJJ (each point moves to its nearest centroid). The update step can only lower JJJ (the mean minimises the sum of squared distances, from ∂J/∂μk=−2∑i∈Ck(x(i)−μk)=0\partial J/\partial\mu_k=-2\sum_{i\in C_k}(x^{(i)}-\mu_k)=0∂J/∂μk​=−2∑i∈Ck​​(x(i)−μk​)=0). JJJ is bounded below by 0, and there are only finitely many possible partitions, so JJJ cannot decrease forever. The algorithm stops once the assignments no longer change. However, JJJ is non-convex, so convergence is to a local minimum that depends on the initial centroids. In practice several runs are made and the lowest-JJJ result is kept.

Source lectureTanvir Sir · Class notes (Class_notes (2).pdf, pp. 137–138)
2022 · Q5(d)Q3.3 — What is the problem associated with the K-Means clustering algorithm?05Topic: limitations

(1) The number of clusters K must be specified in advance. (2) The result depends on the random initial centroids and may be a poor local minimum. (3) It is sensitive to outliers and noise, because the mean is pulled by extreme values. (4) It assumes roughly spherical, equally sized clusters and fails on non-convex shapes or clusters of different density. (5) It is sensitive to feature scaling. (6) It works only with numerical data, and a cluster may become empty. See the table in §3.4.

4. Hierarchical Clustering ★★★

K-means needs the number of clusters KKK fixed in advance. Hierarchical clustering does not. It builds a tree of nested clusters, the dendrogram, from which clusterings for every KKK can be read by cutting the tree at different heights.

4.1 Agglomerative and Divisive Approaches

ApproachHow it works
Agglomerative (HAC), bottom-upStart with every observation as its own cluster (nnn clusters). Repeatedly merge the two closest clusters until one cluster remains. This is the common method and the one examined.
Divisive, top-downStart with all observations in one cluster and repeatedly split a cluster until every observation stands alone. More expensive and rarely used by hand.

4.2 The Dendrogram

Definition
A dendrogram is a tree diagram that records the sequence of merges (or splits) of hierarchical clustering. Each leaf at the bottom is one observation. Each horizontal link joins two clusters, drawn at a height equal to the dissimilarity at which they were merged. Observations that fuse near the bottom are very similar; those that fuse only near the top are very different.
  • Reading it: the similarity of two observations is judged by the height at which their branches first join, not by how close they are horizontally. The left–right order of leaves is arbitrary: a dendrogram can be flipped at any link.
  • Using it: a horizontal cut at height hhh gives the clusters formed by all merges below hhh. The number of vertical lines the cut crosses is the number of clusters. One dendrogram therefore gives every clustering from nnn clusters down to 1.

4.3 Measuring Similarity and Linkage

4.3.1 Dissimilarity between observations

MeasureFormulaNotes
Euclideand(x,y)=∑j(xj−yj)2d(x,y)=\sqrt{\sum_j(x_j-y_j)^2}d(x,y)=∑j​(xj​−yj​)2​Straight-line distance; the default
Manhattan (rectilinear, city-block)d(x,y)=∑j∣xj−yj∣d(x,y)=\sum_j|x_j-y_j|d(x,y)=∑j​∣xj​−yj​∣Sum of axis-wise gaps; less affected by one large difference
Minkowskid=(∑j∣xj−yj∣q)1/qd=\bigl(\sum_j|x_j-y_j|^q\bigr)^{1/q}d=(∑j​∣xj​−yj​∣q)1/qq=1q=1q=1 Manhattan, q=2q=2q=2 Euclidean

4.3.2 Linkage: dissimilarity between clusters

LinkageD(A,B)D(A,B)D(A,B)Behaviour
Single (minimum)min⁡a∈A, b∈Bd(a,b)\min_{a\in A,\,b\in B}d(a,b)mina∈A,b∈B​d(a,b)Nearest pair; finds long, irregular clusters but suffers from chaining

4.4 The HAC Algorithm and the Lecture Example

Agglomerative clustering
  1. Compute the n×nn\times nn×n distance matrix; treat each observation as a cluster.
  2. Find the smallest entry D(A,B)D(A,B)D(A,B) and merge AAA and BBB. Record the merge at height D(A,B)D(A,B)D(A,B) in the dendrogram.
  3. Update the matrix: delete the rows and columns of AAA and BBB and add one for A∪BA\cup BA∪B, with D(A∪B,C)=min⁡{D(A,C),D(B,C)}D(A\cup B,C)=\min\{D(A,C),D(B,C)\}D(A∪B,C)=min{D(A,C),D(B,C)} for single linkage or max⁡{⋅}\max\{\cdot\}max{⋅} for complete linkage.
  4. Repeat steps 2–3 until one cluster remains (n−1n-1n−1 merges), then draw the dendrogram.

4.5 Hierarchical Clustering vs K-Means

AspectHierarchical (agglomerative)K-means
Number of clustersNot needed in advance; chosen afterwards by cutting the dendrogramK must be fixed before running
OutputA nested hierarchy (dendrogram) giving clusterings for every KOne flat partition into K clusters
ProcedureDeterministic sequence of merges; no initialisationIterative, starts from random centroids; result can vary between runs
InputOnly a distance matrix, so any dissimilarity (even non-Euclidean, categorical) can be usedRaw numeric coordinates, to compute means
Cluster shapeDepends on linkage; single linkage finds non-spherical clustersRoughly spherical, similar-size clusters
Revisiting decisionsA merge is never undonePoints can move between clusters at each iteration
ComplexityO(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) memory and O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2)–O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3) time: slow for large nnnO(nKt)O(nKt)O(nKt): fast, scales to large data
InterpretabilityDendrogram shows the relationships at all levels (taxonomies, genes)Centroids summarise each cluster
OutliersAppear as late-joining singletons (easy to spot)Pull centroids and distort clusters

4.6 Choosing the Number of Clusters from a Dendrogram

Cut the dendrogram where the vertical gap between successive merge heights is largest, i.e. across the longest vertical lines that no horizontal link crosses. A large jump in merge height means two clusters that were far apart have been forced together, so the clustering just below the jump is natural. The number of vertical lines crossed by the cut is the optimal number of clusters. Also consider domain knowledge and the purpose of the clustering, the inconsistency coefficient, or silhouette scores.

4.7 Solved Questions

2024 · Q6(a)Q4.1 — Differentiate between Hierarchical clustering and K-Means clustering.10Topic: HC vs K-means

Present the comparison table of §4.5 (number of clusters, output, procedure and initialisation, input, cluster shape, revisiting decisions, complexity, interpretability, outliers), preceded by one-line definitions. K-means partitions nnn observations into a pre-specified number KKK of clusters by iteratively assigning points to the nearest centroid and recomputing centroids. Hierarchical clustering builds a tree of nested clusters by successively merging the closest clusters, visualised as a dendrogram.

Source lectureTanvir Sir · HAC – Hierarchical clustering (MT HAC V3.pdf, pp. 4–8); L1 – Clustering & unsupervised learning (MT_Ml_L1.pdf, pp. 12–13) — Only max/min linkage updates worked; average, centroid and comparison missing
2022 · Q6(a)Q4.3 — What are the advantages of Hierarchical clustering over K-Means clustering? Write down the name of most commonly-used types of linkage for measuring similarity between clusters.10Topic: advantages · linkage types

Advantages over K-means: (1) no need to specify the number of clusters in advance; (2) the dendrogram shows the full hierarchy, so any number of clusters can be read off from one run; (3) deterministic, with no random initialisation and no local-minimum problem from the start; (4) works with any distance or similarity measure, even for non-numeric data, since only a distance matrix is needed; (5) can find non-spherical clusters (single linkage); (6) outliers are easy to spot as late-merging singletons; (7) easy to interpret for small data sets and naturally hierarchical data (biology, document taxonomies).

Common linkage types: single (minimum), complete (maximum), average, centroid, and Ward's minimum-variance linkage.

Source lectureTanvir Sir · HAC – Hierarchical clustering (MT HAC V3.pdf, pp. 4–8); L1 – Clustering & unsupervised learning (MT_Ml_L1.pdf, p. 12) — Advantages not stated; average and centroid linkage missing
2024 · Q6(b)Q4.4 — What is dendrogram, and how is it used in Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering (HAC)? Explain two different ways for measuring similarity among observations.10Topic: dendrogram · similarity measures

Dendrogram: the definition box of §4.2. Use in HAC: each merge of the algorithm is drawn as a horizontal link at the merge distance, building the tree from the leaves up. After clustering, the tree is cut horizontally to obtain the final clusters. The number of vertical lines crossed equals the number of clusters, and the best cut lies across the largest gap in merge heights (§4.6). The dendrogram also shows how similar the groups are (the fusion height) and exposes outliers.

Two ways of measuring similarity among observations:

  1. Euclidean distance d(x,y)=∑j(xj−yj)2d(x,y)=\sqrt{\sum_j(x_j-y_j)^2}d(x,y)=∑j​(xj​−yj​)2​. Two observations are similar if their feature values are close in magnitude. Example: the lecture example, d(P1,P2)=0.23d(P1,P2)=0.23d(P1,P2)=0.23.
  2. Correlation-based distance d(x,y)=1−r(x,y)d(x,y)=1-r(x,y)d(x,y)=1−r(x,y), where rrr is the Pearson correlation of the two observations' feature profiles. Two observations are similar if their features rise and fall together, even when their magnitudes are very different. Example: two customers who buy the same kinds of items in different quantities are similar by correlation but far apart by Euclidean distance.

(Manhattan distance, ∑j∣xj−yj∣\sum_j|x_j-y_j|∑j​∣xj​−yj​∣, is an accepted alternative second measure.)

Source lectureTanvir Sir · HAC – Hierarchical clustering (MT HAC V3.pdf, p. 9); HAC – Hierarchical clustering (MT HAC V3.pdf, pp. 2–3) — Only Euclidean distance shown; correlation-based measure missing
2022 · Q6(c)Q4.5 — How do you find the optimal number of clusters to have upon looking at the dendrogram? Explain with a sketching of random dendrogram.10Topic: cutting a dendrogram

Sketch a dendrogram like Fig. 4.3. Explain the rule of §4.6: (1) look at the heights at which successive merges occur; (2) find the longest vertical distance that no horizontal merge line crosses, which is the largest jump in merge distance; (3) draw a horizontal line through that gap; (4) the number of vertical lines it crosses is the optimal number of clusters (three in Fig. 4.3). Reason: merges below the gap join close observations, while the merge above it joins well-separated groups. Also mention that domain knowledge, the inconsistency coefficient or silhouette analysis can confirm the choice.

5. K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN) ★★★

5.1 The Algorithm

Definition
The K-nearest neighbours classifier assigns a new, unlabeled example the class held by the majority of the K most similar (nearest) labeled examples in the training set. It is very simple but powerful, and well suited to problems where the relationship between features and class is too complex to write down. For regression, the prediction is the average of the K neighbours' target values.
Steps
  1. Store the labeled training set {(xi,yi)}i=1n\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n{(xi​,yi​)}i=1n​. There is no training phase.
  2. Choose the number of neighbours K and a distance function, usually Euclidean: d(x,q)=(x1−q1)2+(x2−q2)2+⋯+(xn−qn)2d(x,q)=\sqrt{(x_1-q_1)^2+(x_2-q_2)^2+\cdots+(x_n-q_n)^2}d(x,q)=(x1​−q1​)2+(x2​−q2​)2+⋯+(xn​−qn​)2​.
  3. For the query point qqq, compute the distance to every training example.
  4. Sort the distances in ascending order and take the K nearest examples.
  5. Vote: the predicted class is the most frequent class among those K (mean value for regression). Optionally weight each vote by 1/d1/d1/d.

Lazy, non-parametric learning. KNN does not build a model or learn parameters. It simply stores the data, so "training" is instant but prediction is slow: every query needs distances to all nnn stored points, O(np)O(np)O(np). It is non-parametric because it makes no assumption about the functional form of the decision boundary.

Assumptions. (1) Similar inputs have similar outputs: points close in feature space tend to share a class (smoothness/locality). (2) The chosen distance metric is meaningful, so all features must be on comparable scales (standardise them). (3) Every feature is relevant: irrelevant features distort distances. (4) There is enough data to populate the neighbourhood of any query, which fails in high dimensions (Chapter 7).

IngredientSweetnessCrunchinessTypeDistance to tomato (6, 4)
apple109fruit(6−10)2+(4−9)2=41=6.403\sqrt{(6-10)^2+(4-9)^2}=\sqrt{41}=6.403(6−10)2+(4−9)2​=41​=6.403
bacon14protein(6−1)2+02=5.000\sqrt{(6-1)^2+0^2}=5.000(6−1)2+02​=5.000

carrot710vegetable1+36=6.083\sqrt{1+36}=6.0831+36​=6.083

k = 1: the nearest distance is 5, shared by bacon and banana (a tie). k = 2: bacon and banana, 50 %–50 % fruit or protein, still undecided. k = 3: bacon, banana and cheese: 2 protein vs 1 fruit, so the tomato is classified as protein. The example shows that the answer depends on K, and that an even K can end in a tie.

5.3 Choosing K

KEffect
Small K (e.g. 1)The decision follows individual points, so noise and outliers have a huge impact. The boundary is very jagged: low bias, high variance → overfitting. Training accuracy is perfect for K = 1.
Large KMany far-away neighbours vote, so the classifier drifts toward predicting the majority class regardless of the local neighbourhood. The boundary is over-smoothed: high bias, low variance → underfitting. With K = n every query gets the global majority class.
Good KBalances the two. Chosen by cross-validation (try K = 1, 3, 5, … and pick the lowest validation error). A common rule of thumb is K≈nK\approx\sqrt nK≈n​, taken odd.
Correction to the KNN slide
The slide states "k is small … this is called underfitting" and "k is large … this is called overfitting". The two labels are swapped. A small K memorises noise (overfitting) and a large K is too smooth (underfitting), as the slide's own descriptions ("noisy data has a huge impact" / "predicts the majority class") show.

Why an odd K? In binary classification an even K can produce a tie (e.g. 2 votes vs 2), which forces an arbitrary tie-break. An odd K always gives a strict majority between two classes. For CCC classes, choose K not divisible by CCC, or break ties by the nearest neighbour or distance weighting.

Other practical points. Standardise features, e.g. z=(x−xˉ)/sz=(x-\bar x)/sz=(x−xˉ)/s or min–max scaling, because a feature measured in large units dominates the distance. Use distance-weighted voting. For big data, speed up the search with KD-trees or ball trees.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Simple and intuitive; no training; naturally multi-class; flexible non-linear boundaries; new data added instantlySlow prediction and high memory use; sensitive to K, scaling, irrelevant features and noise; suffers from the curse of dimensionality; imbalanced classes bias the vote

Applications: optical character recognition, face recognition, recommender systems (will a person enjoy a movie?), finding patterns in genetic data, and fault classification from sensor signatures.

5.4 Solved Questions

2024 · Q7(a)Q5.1 — Explain the K-Nearest Neighbour (KNN) algorithm in detail. Describe its working principle, assumptions, and main steps.10Topic: KNN theory

Working principle: the definition box of §5.1. Classify a new point by the majority class of its K nearest labeled neighbours under a distance metric (Euclidean). It is a lazy, instance-based, non-parametric learner: it stores the data and does all computation at query time. Assumptions: the four listed in §5.1 (locality/smoothness, meaningful and scaled distance, relevant features, enough data density). Main steps: the five steps of §5.1 (store, choose K and metric, compute distances, sort and select K nearest, majority vote). Illustrate with the tomato example (§5.2) and mention the choice of K (§5.3).

Source lectureTanvir Sir · kNN – K-nearest neighbours (MT_kNN_N.pdf, pp. 2–14) — Assumptions (feature scaling, locality) not stated explicitly
2023 · Q7(a)Q5.2 — What is K nearest neighbor (KNN) algorithm? How does the choice of K impact the performance of KNN model?10Topic: KNN · choice of K

KNN: §5.1 (definition + steps). Impact of K: the table of §5.3 and the bias–variance view of Chapter 6. A small K gives a flexible, noisy boundary (low bias, high variance, overfitting). A large K gives a smooth boundary biased toward the majority class (high bias, low variance, underfitting). An even K may cause ties in binary problems. K also affects computation (sorting more neighbours) and robustness to noise. The best K is chosen by cross-validation and is usually odd.

Source lectureTanvir Sir · kNN – K-nearest neighbours (MT_kNN_N.pdf, p. 2); kNN – K-nearest neighbours (MT_kNN_N.pdf, p. 13) — Slide p. 13 swaps the underfitting/overfitting labels
2022 · Q7(a)Q5.3 — What is 'K' in the K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) algorithm and why is the odd value of 'K' preferred over even values in the KNN algorithm?10Topic: K · odd K

K is the number of nearest labeled training examples (neighbours) that are consulted, and that vote, when classifying a new point. It is the single hyper-parameter of KNN and controls the smoothness of the decision boundary (§5.3).

Why odd: with two classes, an even K can split the votes equally (e.g. K = 2 → 1 : 1, K = 4 → 2 : 2), leaving the class undecided. The tomato example shows this: at k = 2 the vote is 50 %–50 %. An odd K always gives a strict majority between two classes, so the decision is unique without an arbitrary tie-breaking rule. Odd K is therefore preferred for binary classification. For more classes it reduces but does not eliminate ties.

6. The Bias–Variance Trade-off ★★★

6.1 Bias and Variance

Definitions
Suppose the data are generated as y=f(x)+εy=f(x)+\varepsilony=f(x)+ε with E[ε]=0E[\varepsilon]=0E[ε]=0, Var(ε)=σ2\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon)=\sigma^2Var(ε)=σ2, and a model f^\hat ff^​ is learned from a random training set.
  • Bias =E[f^(x)]−f(x)=E[\hat f(x)]-f(x)=E[f^​(x)]−f(x): the error from wrong or too-simple assumptions. It measures how far the average model (over many training sets) is from the truth. High bias means the model misses real patterns: underfitting.
  • Variance =E[(f^(x)−E[f^(x)])2]=E\bigl[(\hat f(x)-E[\hat f(x)])^2\bigr]=E[(f^​(x)−E[f^​(x)])2]: how much the learned model changes when trained on a different sample. High variance means the model follows the noise of its particular training set: overfitting.
  • Irreducible error σ2\sigma^2σ2: noise in the data that no model can remove.

Fix a test point xxx and write f=f(x)f=f(x)f=f(x) and f^=f^(x)\hat f=\hat f(x)f^​=f^​(x). The noise ε\varepsilonε is independent of f^\hat ff^​.

Add and subtract fˉ=E[f^]\bar f=E[\hat f]fˉ​=E[f^​]: E[(f−f^)2]=E[(f−fˉ+fˉ−f^)2]=(f−fˉ)2+E[(f^−fˉ)2]+2(f−fˉ) E[fˉ−f^]E[(f-\hat f)^2]=E[(f-\bar f+\bar f-\hat f)^2]=(f-\bar f)^2+E[(\hat f-\bar f)^2]+2(f-\bar f)\,E[\bar f-\hat f]E[(f−f^​)2]=E[(f−fˉ​+fˉ​−f^​)2]=(f−fˉ​)2+E[(f^​−fˉ​)2]+2(f−fˉ​)E[fˉ​−f^​].

6.3 The Trade-off

As model complexity grows (more features, higher polynomial degree, deeper trees, smaller K in KNN), bias falls but variance rises. Total test error is therefore U-shaped. The best model sits at the bottom of the U, where the sum is smallest. You cannot minimise both at once, hence a trade-off.

High bias (underfit)High variance (overfit)
Training errorHighVery low
Test errorHigh (≈ training)High (≫ training)
ModelToo simple (linear fit to a curve, K = n)Too complex (degree-15 polynomial, K = 1)
FixMore features, more complex model, less regularisationMore data, fewer features, regularisation, pruning, larger K, cross-validation, ensembles (bagging)

6.4 Solved Question

2023 · Q6(a)Q6.1 — Explain the concept of bias-variance trade-off in machine learning. How does it affect model performance?10Topic: bias–variance

Concept. The expected prediction error of a model splits into three parts, Bias² + Variance + irreducible noise (state the formula of §6.2, with the four-line derivation if time allows). Bias is the error from overly simple assumptions: the model is consistently wrong in the same way. Variance is the error from sensitivity to the particular training sample: the model changes a lot from one data set to another. Making a model more flexible reduces bias but increases variance, and vice versa. This opposing behaviour is the bias–variance trade-off (Fig. 6.1).

Effect on performance.

  • High bias → underfitting: poor accuracy on both training and test data. Example: a straight line fitted to curved data, or KNN with a very large K.
  • High variance → overfitting: near-perfect training accuracy but poor test accuracy (poor generalisation). Example: a very deep decision tree, or KNN with K = 1.
  • Balanced model: the lowest test error. It generalises best.

Managing it: choose model complexity (and hyper-parameters such as K, tree depth or λ) by cross-validation; use regularisation (ridge/lasso) and pruning; gather more training data, which lowers variance; reduce dimensionality (Chapter 7); use ensembles (bagging and random forests reduce variance; boosting reduces bias).

Source lectureTanvir Sir · Class notes (Class_notes (2).pdf, pp. 106–112)

7. Curse of Dimensionality and Dimensionality Reduction ★★★

7.1 The Curse of Dimensionality

Definition (lecture)
The curse of dimensionality is a phenomenon that arises when working with high-dimensional data sets. As the number of features (dimensions) increases, the volume of the feature space grows exponentially, so the amount of data needed to cover it also grows exponentially. The data become sparse, and patterns become harder to find. A high-dimensional data set needs far more samples to reach the same accuracy as a low-dimensional one.

How fast the demand grows. Suppose 10 sample values per feature are enough to describe a feature well. One feature needs 101010 samples, two features need 102=10010^2=100102=100 to fill the square at the same density, three need 10310^3103, and ddd features need 10d10^d10d. With d=20d=20d=20, even 101210^{12}1012 samples would only match the density of 10 points on a line.

Neighbourhoods stop being local. In the unit hypercube [0,1]d[0,1]^d[0,1]d, a sub-cube that contains 10 % of uniformly spread data must have edge length e=0.11/de=0.1^{1/d}e=0.11/d: e=0.10e=0.10e=0.10 for d=1d=1d=1, 0.320.320.32 for d=2d=2d=2, 0.790.790.79 for d=10d=10d=10 and 0.980.980.98 for d=100d=100d=100. To collect only 10 % of the data, a "neighbourhood" must span almost the whole range of every feature. KNN's "nearest" neighbours are no longer near.

Distances concentrate. For random points in high dimension, the distances from a query to its nearest and to its farthest neighbour become almost equal: (dmax−dmin)/dmin→0(d_{max}-d_{min})/d_{min}\to0(dmax​−dmin​)/dmin​→0 as d→∞d\to\inftyd→∞. Distance-based methods (KNN, K-means, hierarchical clustering) lose their power to discriminate.

7.2 The Empty Space Phenomenon

Definition
The empty space phenomenon is the fact that high-dimensional spaces are inherently sparse: with any realistic number of samples, almost all of the space contains no data. Moreover, the volume, and hence the data, concentrates in regions that intuition from 2-D and 3-D would call "empty": the corners of a cube and a thin outer shell of a sphere, far from the centre.

Calculation 1: the inscribed ball vanishes. The volume of a ddd-dimensional ball of radius rrr is Vball=πd/2Γ(d/2+1)rdV_{ball}=\dfrac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(d/2+1)}r^dVball​=Γ(d/2+1)πd/2​rd. The cube around it has side 2r2r2r and volume (2r)d(2r)^d(2r)d. Their ratio is

VballVcube=πd/22d Γ(d/2+1)\frac{V_{ball}}{V_{cube}}=\frac{\pi^{d/2}}{2^d\,\Gamma(d/2+1)}Vcube​Vball​​=2dΓ(d/2+1)πd/2​ d=2: π4=0.785,d=3: π6=0.524,d=10: 0.0025,d=20: 2.5×10−8.d=2:\ \frac{\pi}{4}=0.785,\quad d=3:\ \frac{\pi}{6}=0.524,\quad d=10:\ 0.0025,\quad d=20:\ 2.5\times10^{-8}.d=2: 4π​=0.785,d=3: 6π​=0.524,d=10: 0.0025,d=20: 2.5×10−8.

In 20 dimensions, virtually all of the cube's volume lies in its corners, outside the central ball. Uniform data placed in the cube are almost all "far from the centre".

Calculation 2: the volume lives in the skin. The fraction of a ball's volume within a thin outer shell of relative thickness ϵ\epsilonϵ is

V(r)−V(r(1−ϵ))V(r)=1−(1−ϵ)d.\frac{V(r)-V(r(1-\epsilon))}{V(r)}=1-(1-\epsilon)^d .V(r)V(r)−V(r(1−ϵ))​=1−(1−ϵ)d.

For ϵ=0.1\epsilon=0.1ϵ=0.1: 19 % when d=2d=2d=2, 65 % when d=10d=10d=10, 88 % when d=20d=20d=20 and 99.997 % when d=100d=100d=100. A standard Gaussian in high dimension similarly has almost no samples near its mean: they concentrate on a shell of radius about d\sqrt dd​.

Why it is a direct indication of the curse. The curse of dimensionality is the exponential growth of volume. The empty space phenomenon is what that growth looks like for a fixed amount of data: the same nnn points become ever more isolated, every point is far from every other and from the centre, and local neighbourhoods are empty. Anything that relies on density or on nearby examples (KNN, kernel density estimation, clustering, local regression) starts to fail. Its only cure is exponentially more data, or reducing the number of dimensions.

7.3 Curse of Dimensionality and Overfitting

  • Too many parameters for the data: a model with ppp features has at least ppp parameters. When ppp approaches or exceeds nnn, it can fit the training set perfectly. For example, linear regression with p=np=np=n interpolates every point, including its noise, so the model fits noise rather than signal.
  • Sparse data, spurious patterns: in a nearly empty space, random fluctuations look like structure. With many irrelevant or redundant features some will correlate with the target by chance, and the model uses them.
  • Peaking (Hughes) phenomenon: for a fixed number of training samples, accuracy first improves as features are added and then deteriorates once the extra dimensions add more variance than information.
  • Result: low training error, high test error, i.e. high variance and poor generalisation (Chapter 6).
  • Mitigation (lecture): dimensionality reduction, feature selection and regularisation reduce the effective number of features and hence the model's complexity.

7.4 Dimensionality Reduction

Definition
Dimensionality reduction is the process of transforming high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional space that still preserves the essence of the original data. It reduces the number of features while retaining as much of the important information (variance, structure, class separability) as possible, either by selecting a subset of the original features or by creating new features that combine them.

7.4.1 Positive aspects (lecture)

  1. Less storage: the space needed to store the data shrinks with the number of dimensions.
  2. Less computation: fewer dimensions mean faster training and prediction.
  3. Algorithms work better: some algorithms perform poorly in high dimensions (KNN, clustering, density estimation), so reducing dimensions makes them usable.
  4. Removes multicollinearity: redundant, highly correlated features are merged. The lecture's example is "time on treadmill" and "calories burnt": one of them carries the information of both.
  5. Visualisation: projecting to 2-D or 3-D lets us plot and see clusters and patterns.
  6. Less overfitting and noise: discarding low-variance directions often removes noise and improves generalisation.

7.4.2 Two main approaches

AspectFeature selectionFeature extraction
IdeaChoose a subset of the original features most relevant to the problemCreate new features by combining or transforming the originals
ResultOriginal, interpretable features kept (e.g. keep "temperature", drop "day of week")New composite features (e.g. PC1 = 0.59 × systolic + 0.81 × diastolic)
MethodsFilter (rank features by correlation, chi-square or mutual information with the target) · Wrapper (forward/backward selection, judged by model performance) · Embedded (selection during training: lasso, tree importance)Linear: PCA, LDA, factor analysis, ICA · Non-linear: t-SNE, LLE, Isomap, UMAP, autoencoders, kernel PCA
InformationDiscarded features are lost completelyInformation from all features is compressed into the new ones
ExampleFrom 500 sensor channels, keep the 20 most correlated with machine failureCombine two blood-pressure readings into one PCA score (Q8.4)

7.4.3 Linear and non-linear techniques

Linear techniques find a linear transformation to a lower-dimensional space. PCA maximises the variance of the projected data. LDA maximises class separation. Factor analysis and ICA are the others. Non-linear techniques find a non-linear mapping. t-SNE is the most popular, especially for visualisation; LLE, Isomap and UMAP preserve the geometry of curved manifolds.

7.5 Solved Questions

2024 · Q7(c)Q7.1 — Define empty space phenomenon and explain why it is considered a direct indication of the curse of dimensionality.10Topic: empty space phenomenon

Definition: the box in §7.2. High-dimensional spaces are inherently sparse, so a fixed data set occupies almost none of the space, and the volume is concentrated in the corners and outer shells, far from the centre.

Explanation, with the two calculations of §7.2: (i) the ratio of a ball's volume to that of its bounding cube falls from 0.785 (2-D) and 0.524 (3-D) to 0.0025 (10-D); (ii) the outer 10 % shell of a ball holds 65 % of its volume in 10-D and 88 % in 20-D. So data spread in a high-dimensional space are nearly all far from the centre and from each other.

Why it indicates the curse: the curse of dimensionality means the space grows exponentially with ddd while the data do not. The empty space phenomenon is the direct, measurable result: neighbourhoods are empty, distances between points become large and nearly equal, and density-based or distance-based learners (KNN, clustering) lose meaning. Covering the space would need exponentially many samples (10d at 10 per axis), and that is exactly the curse. The practical remedies are dimensionality reduction and feature selection.

Source lectureTanvir Sir · L2 – Dimensionality reduction (MT_Ml_L.pdf, p. 5); L2 – Dimensionality reduction (MT_Ml_L.pdf, p. 3) — Term only named in syllabus; sparsity explained on p. 5
2023 · Q7(c)Q7.2 — What is meant by curse of dimensionality? Explain how it can lead machine learning model to overfitting.10Topic: curse · overfitting

Meaning: the definition of §7.1, supported by the 10d10^d10d sample-count argument and the 10 % neighbourhood edge length (0.11/d0.1^{1/d}0.11/d). How it leads to overfitting: the four points of §7.3. (1) The number of parameters grows with the features, and when p≳np\gtrsim np≳n the model can fit the training data, noise included. (2) Sparse data create spurious correlations with irrelevant features. (3) The peaking phenomenon: for fixed nnn, accuracy falls after too many features. (4) The result is low training error and high test error, i.e. high variance. Remedies: dimensionality reduction (PCA), feature selection, regularisation and more data.

Source lectureTanvir Sir · L2 – Dimensionality reduction (MT_Ml_L.pdf, pp. 5–6)
2022 · Q7(c)Q7.3 — Briefly explain the curse of dimensionality problem.10Topic: curse of dimensionality

As the number of features ddd grows, the volume of the feature space grows exponentially, so a fixed amount of data becomes sparse. To keep the same sampling density, 10 values per feature need 10d10^d10d samples. Consequences: (1) neighbourhoods are no longer local (a cube holding 10 % of the data needs an edge of 0.79 of each axis in 10-D); (2) distances between points concentrate, making nearest and farthest neighbours almost equally far, which harms KNN and clustering; (3) most data lie near the boundary, the empty space phenomenon; (4) models with many features overfit, and computation and storage grow. The remedies are dimensionality reduction (PCA, LDA), feature selection, regularisation and more data.

Definition: the box of §7.4. Why essential: it fights the curse of dimensionality and overfitting, and gives the benefits of §7.4.1 (storage, computation, algorithm performance, multicollinearity, visualisation, noise removal). Two approaches: the table of §7.4.2. Feature selection keeps a subset of the original features (filter, wrapper, embedded); example: selecting the 20 most failure-related of 500 sensor channels. Feature extraction builds new features from combinations of the originals; example: PCA combining systolic and diastolic blood pressure into one component (Q8.4).

2022 · Q8(c)Q7.6 — Briefly explain the two main approaches to dimensionality reduction: (i) Feature selection, (ii) Feature extraction.05Topic: selection vs extraction

(i) Feature selection chooses a subset of the original features most relevant to the problem, keeping the crucial ones and dropping the rest. Filter methods rank features by their relation to the target; wrapper methods choose features by how well a model performs with them; embedded methods pick features while training (e.g. lasso). The selected features keep their original meaning.

(ii) Feature extraction creates new features by combining or transforming the originals, capturing the essence of the data in fewer dimensions. Examples are PCA (projection that preserves maximum variance), LDA and t-SNE. The new features are compact but less directly interpretable.

8. Covariance and Principal Component Analysis ★★★

8.1 Variance, Covariance and Correlation

Definitions
Variance measures the spread of one variable about its mean:  var(X)=∑i=1n(Xi−Xˉ)2n−1\ \mathrm{var}(X)=\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\bar X)^2}{n-1} var(X)=n−1∑i=1n​(Xi​−Xˉ)2​.
Covariance measures how two variables vary together about their means: cov(X,Y)=∑i=1n(Xi−Xˉ)(Yi−Yˉ)n−1.\mathrm{cov}(X,Y)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i-\bar X)(Y_i-\bar Y)}{n-1}.cov(X,Y)=n−1∑i=1n​(Xi​−Xˉ)(Yi​−Yˉ)​. Correlation (Pearson) is covariance scaled to lie between −1 and +1: rXY=cov(X,Y)σX σY,−1≤r≤1.r_{XY}=\frac{\mathrm{cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_X\,\sigma_Y},\qquad-1\le r\le1.rXY​=σX​σY​cov(X,Y)​,−1≤r≤1.
  • The covariance of a variable with itself is its variance: cov(X,X)=var(X)\mathrm{cov}(X,X)=\mathrm{var}(X)cov(X,X)=var(X).
  • Sign matters more than size: positive covariance means both increase together (hours studied and marks); negative means one rises as the other falls; zero means no linear relationship (height and marks).
  • The magnitude of covariance depends on units (cm vs m), so it is hard to interpret. Correlation removes the units: r=±1r=\pm1r=±1 is a perfect linear relation, and r=0r=0r=0 means no linear relation.
AspectCovarianceCorrelation
MeasuresDirection of the joint variabilityDirection and strength of the linear relationship
Range−∞-\infty−∞ to +∞+\infty+∞−1-1−1 to +1+1+1
UnitsProduct of the two variables' unitsDimensionless
Scale changeChanges if units changeUnaffected by linear scaling
UseBuilding block of PCA (covariance matrix)Comparing relationships; PCA on standardised data uses the correlation matrix

8.2 The Covariance Matrix

For ppp variables, collect every pairwise covariance in a p×pp\times pp×p matrix. For three dimensions:

C=[cov(x,x)cov(x,y)cov(x,z)cov(y,x)cov(y,y)cov(y,z)cov(z,x)cov(z,y)cov(z,z)].C=\begin{bmatrix}\mathrm{cov}(x,x)&\mathrm{cov}(x,y)&\mathrm{cov}(x,z)\\\mathrm{cov}(y,x)&\mathrm{cov}(y,y)&\mathrm{cov}(y,z)\\\mathrm{cov}(z,x)&\mathrm{cov}(z,y)&\mathrm{cov}(z,z)\end{bmatrix}.C=​cov(x,x)cov(y,x)cov(z,x)​cov(x,y)cov(y,y)cov(z,y)​cov(x,z)cov(y,z)cov(z,z)​​.

The diagonal holds the variances. Because cov(x,y)=cov(y,x)\mathrm{cov}(x,y)=\mathrm{cov}(y,x)cov(x,y)=cov(y,x), the matrix is symmetric, so its eigenvalues are real and its eigenvectors orthogonal. It is also positive semidefinite, so all eigenvalues are ≥ 0. With the mean-centred data matrix ZZZ (n×pn\times pn×p), C=ZTZn−1C=\dfrac{Z^TZ}{n-1}C=n−1ZTZ​.

Why not just plot? For two variables a scatter plot shows the relationship, but real data have many dimensions (often more than 3), where visualisation is impossible. Covariance quantifies every pairwise relationship numerically in any number of dimensions, and the covariance matrix feeds directly into algorithms such as PCA.

8.3 Principal Component Analysis

Definition
PCA is a linear transformation that chooses a new orthogonal coordinate system for the data such that the greatest variance of any projection lies on the first axis (the first principal component), the second greatest on the second axis, and so on. Dimensionality is reduced by dropping the later components, which carry little variance.

Lecture toy example. The six 3-D points (1, 2, 3), (2, 4, 6), (4, 8, 12), (3, 6, 9), (5, 10, 15) and (6, 12, 18) need 18 bytes at one byte per component. All of them are multiples of (1, 2, 3): they lie on one line, a 1-D subspace of 3-D space. Storing the direction (3 bytes) and one coefficient per point (6 bytes) needs only 9 bytes, a 50 % saving with no loss. PCA finds such directions automatically. Here the covariance matrix has a single non-zero eigenvalue, whose eigenvector is along (1, 2, 3).

8.3.1 Derivation: PCA is an eigenvalue problem

  1. Mean-centre the data, zi=xi−xˉz_i=x_i-\bar xzi​=xi​−xˉ. Project onto a unit vector www: the projected values are wTziw^Tz_iwTzi​.
  2. Their variance is 1n−1∑i(wTzi)2=1n−1∑iwTziziTw=wT(1n−1∑iziziT)w=wTCw\dfrac{1}{n-1}\sum_i(w^Tz_i)^2=\dfrac{1}{n-1}\sum_iw^Tz_iz_i^Tw=w^T\Bigl(\dfrac{1}{n-1}\sum_iz_iz_i^T\Bigr)w=w^TCwn−11​∑i​(wTzi​)2=n−11​∑i​wTzi​ziT​w=wT(n−11​∑i​zi​ziT​)w=wTCw.
  3. Maximise wTCww^TCwwTCw subject to wTw=1w^Tw=1wTw=1. Lagrangian: L=wTCw−λ(wTw−1)L=w^TCw-\lambda(w^Tw-1)L=wTCw−λ(wTw−1).
  4. ∇wL=2Cw−2λw=0 ⇒ Cw=λw\nabla_wL=2Cw-2\lambda w=0\ \Rightarrow\ \boxed{Cw=\lambda w}∇w​L=2Cw−2λw=0 ⇒ Cw=λw​: www must be an eigenvector of CCC.
  5. The variance captured is then wTCw=wT(λw)=λ wTw=λw^TCw=w^T(\lambda w)=\lambda\,w^Tw=\lambdawTCw=wT(λw)=λwTw=λ. The maximum variance is the largest eigenvalue, and PC1 is its eigenvector.
  6. The second PC maximises variance subject to being orthogonal to PC1, which gives the eigenvector of the second-largest eigenvalue, and so on.
  7. Total variance =trace(C)=∑kλk=\mathrm{trace}(C)=\sum_k\lambda_k=trace(C)=∑k​λk​. The share explained by PC kkk is λk/∑jλj\lambda_k/\sum_j\lambda_jλk​/∑j​λj​.
PCA procedure (lecture steps)
  1. Subtract the mean of each dimension. This moves the origin to the centre of the data.
  2. Compute the covariance matrix C=ZTZ/(n−1)C=Z^TZ/(n-1)C=ZTZ/(n−1).
  3. Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of CCC (unit length).
  4. Form the feature vector: sort eigenvectors by decreasing eigenvalue and keep the top kkk (here k=1k=1k=1).
  5. Derive the new data: FinalData = RowFeatureVector × RowZeroMeanData, i.e. score =vT(x−xˉ)=v^T(x-\bar x)=vT(x−xˉ) for each point.
2 × 2 eigenvalues and eigenvectors by hand
For C=[abbc]C=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{bmatrix}C=[ab​bc​]:  det⁡(C−λI)=λ2−(a+c)λ+(ac−b2)=0\ \det(C-\lambda I)=\lambda^2-(a+c)\lambda+(ac-b^2)=0 det(C−λI)=λ2−(a+c)λ+(ac−b2)=0, so λ1,2=(a+c)±(a+c)2−4(ac−b2)2.\lambda_{1,2}=\frac{(a+c)\pm\sqrt{(a+c)^2-4(ac-b^2)}}{2}.λ1,2​=2(a+c)±(a+c)2−4(ac−b2)​​. Eigenvector for λ\lambdaλ: from the first row, (a−λ)v1+bv2=0⇒v∝[bλ−a](a-\lambda)v_1+bv_2=0\Rightarrow v\propto\begin{bmatrix}b\\\lambda-a\end{bmatrix}(a−λ)v1​+bv2​=0⇒v∝[bλ−a​]. Divide by its length to get a unit vector.

8.3.2 Why the covariance matrix is necessary for PCA

  • PCA seeks directions of maximum variance. The variance of the data along any direction www is wTCww^TCwwTCw, so CCC contains all the information about spread in every direction (derivation step 2).
  • The principal components are the eigenvectors of CCC, and their importance is given by its eigenvalues. Without CCC there is nothing to diagonalise.
  • The off-diagonal covariances measure redundancy (correlation) between features. PCA exploits exactly this redundancy: strongly correlated features collapse into one component.
  • In the new axes the covariance matrix becomes diagonal: the principal components are uncorrelated. This is the goal of the transformation.

8.3.3 Limitations of PCA for non-linear data

  • Only linear projections: PCA can only rotate and project. Data lying on a curved manifold (a Swiss roll, concentric circles, a spiral) cannot be "unfolded", and nearby points on the manifold may be projected far apart or on top of each other.
  • Variance ≠ importance: the direction of largest variance may not be the one that separates classes or carries the structure. Non-linear structure can have low linear variance.
  • Captures only linear correlation (second-order statistics); higher-order, non-linear dependence is ignored.
  • Orthogonality constraint: components must be perpendicular, which rarely matches curved structure.
  • It is also sensitive to scaling and outliers, and its components are hard to interpret.

Alternatives: Kernel PCA (PCA in a kernel-induced feature space: RBF or polynomial) · t-SNE (preserves local neighbourhoods; excellent for visualisation) · UMAP · Isomap (geodesic distances on the manifold) · Locally Linear Embedding (LLE) · Autoencoders (neural-network non-linear compression) · LDA when class labels exist.

2022 · Q8(a)Q8.1 — Write short notes on: (i) Covariance, (ii) Correlation. Why is it necessary to compute a covariance matrix for Principle Component Analysis?10Topic: covariance · correlation · PCA

(i) Covariance: formula, meaning of sign (positive, negative, zero), covariance with itself = variance, and the unit dependence of its magnitude (§8.1). Example: hours studied vs marks gives a positive covariance. (ii) Correlation: r=cov/(σXσY)r=\mathrm{cov}/(\sigma_X\sigma_Y)r=cov/(σX​σY​), dimensionless, from −1 to +1, measuring the strength and direction of a linear relationship; include the comparison table. Why a covariance matrix for PCA: the four points of §8.3.2. It holds the variance along every direction (wTCww^TCwwTCw), its eigenvectors are the principal components and its eigenvalues their variances, its off-diagonals capture the redundancy that PCA removes, and diagonalising it gives uncorrelated components.

Why calculate covariance: (1) a plot works only for 2, at most 3, dimensions, while real data sets have many features, and covariance measures relationships between every pair of dimensions in high-dimensional data where visualisation is impossible; (2) it gives an objective number (sign and magnitude) rather than a visual impression, which can be compared and used in computation; (3) the covariance matrix is the input to algorithms such as PCA, LDA and Gaussian models, which a picture cannot feed. ∑(x1−xˉ1)2=2.25+0.25+0.25+2.25=5\sum(x_1-\bar x_1)^2=2.25+0.25+0.25+2.25=5∑(x1​−xˉ1​)2=2.25+0.25+0.25+2.25=5;  ∑(x2−xˉ2)2=9+1+1+9=20\ \sum(x_2-\bar x_2)^2=9+1+1+9=20 ∑(x2​−xˉ2​)2=9+1+1+9=20;  ∑(x1−xˉ1)(x2−xˉ2)=4.5+0.5+0.5+4.5=10\ \sum(x_1-\bar x_1)(x_2-\bar x_2)=4.5+0.5+0.5+4.5=10 ∑(x1​−xˉ1​)(x2​−xˉ2​)=4.5+0.5+0.5+4.5=10.

Step 3: covariance matrix.

C=13[5101020]=[1.6673.3333.3336.667]C=\frac13\begin{bmatrix}5&10\\10&20\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1.667&3.333\\3.333&6.667\end{bmatrix}C=31​[510​1020​]=[1.6673.333​3.3336.667​]

Step 4: eigenvalues. det⁡(C−λI)=λ2−tr(C)λ+det⁡C\det(C-\lambda I)=\lambda^2-\mathrm{tr}(C)\lambda+\det Cdet(C−λI)=λ2−tr(C)λ+detC, with trC=253=8.333\mathrm{tr}C=\tfrac{25}{3}=8.333trC=325​=8.333 and det⁡C=53⋅203−(103)2=1009−1009=0\det C=\tfrac{5}{3}\cdot\tfrac{20}{3}-\left(\tfrac{10}{3}\right)^2=\tfrac{100}{9}-\tfrac{100}{9}=0detC=35​⋅320​−(310​)2=9100​−9100​=0.

λ2−8.333λ=0 ⇒ λ(λ−8.333)=0 ⇒ λ1=8.333,λ2=0.\lambda^2-8.333\lambda=0\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda(\lambda-8.333)=0\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda_1=8.333,\quad\lambda_2=0.λ2−8.333λ=0 ⇒ λ(λ−8.333)=0 ⇒ λ1​=8.333,λ2​=0.

Step 5: eigenvector of λ1\lambda_1λ1​. (1.667−8.333)v1+3.333v2=0⇒v2=2v1⇒v1=15(1,2)=(0.447, 0.894)(1.667-8.333)v_1+3.333v_2=0\Rightarrow v_2=2v_1\Rightarrow v_1=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(1,2)=(0.447,\ 0.894)(1.667−8.333)v1​+3.333v2​=0⇒v2​=2v1​⇒v1​=5​1​(1,2)=(0.447, 0.894).

[INTUITION]x2=2x1x_2=2x_1x2​=2x1​ exactly: every point lies on the line through the mean with direction (1, 2). All the variance is along that line, and none across it, so one eigenvalue is 0.

With population covariance (divide by 4): C=[1.252.52.55]C=\begin{bmatrix}1.25&2.5\\2.5&5\end{bmatrix}C=[1.252.5​2.55​], λ=6.25, 0\lambda=6.25,\,0λ=6.25,0. Same conclusion.

Eigenvalues: λ₁ = 8.333, λ₂ = 0. λ₁ corresponds to PC1 (direction (0.447, 0.894))

Why λ₁ is the first principal component: the variance of the data projected onto an eigenvector equals its eigenvalue (wTCw=λw^TCw=\lambdawTCw=λ, §8.3.1). PC1 is by definition the direction of maximum variance, so it belongs to the largest eigenvalue, λ1=8.333\lambda_1=8.333λ1​=8.333. It explains 8.333/8.333=100 %8.333/8.333=100\,\%8.333/8.333=100% of the variance, since λ2=0\lambda_2=0λ2​=0 means no spread perpendicular to the line. The data are therefore exactly one-dimensional, and projecting onto PC1 loses no information.
